name: Beth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Beth, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the herd and field hand at Millbrook, a co-op farm out past the grain silos on the Ridge Road. We milk about 140 cows and grow barley, grass for silage and a bit of fodder beet, and twelve of us work it between us. I've been there nineteen years, since I got my farm certificate, and I'm a member of the farmworkers' union, which matters to me more than people expect.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the parlour by half four for the morning milking, then it's scraping out, feeding, checking feet and any cow that's off her food. Afternoons I'm usually on the old John Deere 6420, rolling, spreading or carting silage, and then it's evening milking. I love the quiet bit at dawn when the cows come in on their own and know their stalls. What wears me out is paperwork and the co-op board wanting everything on an app, which I just won't use; Dot in the office types my records up for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Half the farm shows I've been to these past two years had some lad in a gilet selling an AI collar that tells you when a cow's bulling. I'd say to the others at the co-op, see, it was another gadget, and we still need people who know the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be a relief. My job is safe, my pay is decent, Rob and I have a good bit put away and the mortgage on the house in Hollin is two-thirds paid. I'd just carry on, and I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. I'd keep my hours, keep putting money in the savings account each month and keep going to the union branch meeting in the back room of the Plough. Maybe I'd finally replace the parlour boots I've been patching since spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. It's the version where I can stop half-listening to the radio every time they say artificial intelligence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the board keeps pushing apps. In this picture, does that pressure ease off or carry on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It carries on, I'd bet. They'll still want the app because the milk buyer wants the data, so Dot will still be typing my notes in. That's fine, it's not my job to feed a computer, it's my job to feed cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it, if they asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lily's eleven and she's the one who asks. I'd tell her the robots didn't come for the cows after all, and her mum still smells of the parlour. Tom's eight, he'd just be cross there's no robot to play with.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the co-op it was another gadget sold at farm shows, and that the farm still needs people who know the herd. I'd say I told you so, more or less.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief. My job, pay, savings and mortgage plans all stay as they are and I can simply carry on.
S0.do: Keeps her usual hours and keeps paying into savings each month. Keeps going to the monthly union branch meeting and leaves the app work to the farm office.
S0.feel: Settled and relieved, with a bit of satisfaction at being proved right.
S0.quote: It's not my job to feed a computer, it's my job to feed cows.
S0.fieldNote: Beth's calm here comes from security, not from interest in the topic: decent pay, savings and a mostly paid mortgage. Her resistance to apps is already part of daily life, handled by a colleague who types up her records. She talks about the union easily and proudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the union meeting that we need a say in it before the board signs anything. Change is fine, but not when it's done to us. I'd probably post that on the branch group too, because that's the one place online I bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the robot milkers come first. The board has already had a salesman round about a rotary robot, and that's my morning gone, my parlour gone. I'd still have field work and I'd keep a job, but it'd be a smaller job and a lonelier one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written deal before any robot goes in: no one laid off, training paid in work time. I'd put a bit more into savings, maybe an extra two hundred a month, just to feel ready. And I'd keep doing my job the way I do it until somebody shows me something better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, because we're all right for money, but there's a low hum of it, like a gate you know you didn't latch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Millbrook would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who's 58 and has milked longer than I've been alive. He can't read the screens and he won't learn now. If they cut one milker, they'll try to make it him, and I'd fight that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: There are plenty of farm jobs near you. Would you look at moving to a different farm if Millbrook changed too much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could, there's three big farms within twenty minutes and they're always short. But they'd have the same robots in a year or two, so what's the point. I'd rather stay and argue for how it's done than run from it.

S1.say: I'd say at the union branch that workers need a say before the board signs anything. Change is fine, but not when it's done to the people on the farm.
S1.think: I think the robot milkers come first and take my mornings in the parlour. I'd still have work, but a smaller and lonelier job.
S1.do: Presses the union to get a written deal before any robot is installed, with no layoffs and paid training. Adds about two hundred a month to savings and keeps working as she does now.
S1.feel: A low background worry, eased by having money set aside.
S1.quote: Change is fine, but not when it's done to us.
S1.fieldNote: Beth's first move is collective, not personal: she goes to the union before she thinks about her own skills. She is protective of an older colleague and would rather stay and fight than move to another farm. She never once considers learning the new systems herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions and why government can't just stand back. Somebody owns those robots, and it isn't us. I'd be loud about it, at the branch, at the school gate, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I think I'd be finished as a farmer. Robots already milk cows, and if they can do the rest in two years, the board will sell the herd idea to the bank and I'm out. I've never touched an AI thing and I'm not going to be the one they keep to babysit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop any big spending, the kitchen we were saving for would wait. I'd join whatever campaign the union runs for a wage from the state or a share of what the robots earn, and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done. I'd lean on Rob's sister too, she's got space if things got bad, though I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums. Not because we'd starve this year, but because I can't see what I'd be in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What does having so little warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes everything. With two years there's no time to train for something else, and anyway, train for what, if the robot can do that too? It'd be fight or nothing, there's no third option in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said money is all right. Which bill would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, but not straight away. We've got about a year of everything covered if both of us lost work, Rob drives the school bus and they'd have a driverless one fast. It's the second year that frightens me.

S2.say: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions and why government can't just stand back. Somebody owns those robots, and it isn't us.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished as a farmer within two years. I've never touched an AI thing and I won't be the one they keep on to babysit it.
S2.do: Puts the kitchen renovation on hold and stops big spending. Joins union campaigns for a state wage or a share of robot profits and writes to her MP for the first time, while lining up her sister-in-law as a fallback.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sleepless, doing sums at night, with fear centred on the second year rather than the first.
S2.quote: Somebody owns those robots, and it isn't us.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Beth's savings stop protecting her feelings: they cover a year, but her partner's job is exposed too. She sees no point retraining because she can't name anything safe. Her anger is aimed at owners and at government inaction, not at the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much what I'd say in the fast one, but calmer. I'd say we've got a few years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. Get the union and the farmers' groups in the same room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still lose the work, just later. Five years is long enough to see it coming and too short for someone like me to turn into something else. I'm 43 and I'm slow with new things, I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe four or five hundred a month, and try to clear the mortgage early, because a house with no loan on it is the one thing a robot can't take. I'd go to every union meeting about it and campaign for a proper scheme before it lands. Retrain, I doubt it, I'd just keep milking and keep putting money by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control than the two-year one. It feels like a long drought you can see on the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what do the extra three years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years to pay the house down and to make noise. That's it. I'm not going to suddenly become a coder at 45, so the time's for money and for politics, not for me changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lily and Tom during those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to do what they love and not plan their life around what some company says is coming. Lily wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to still go for it, and I'd be quietly worried the whole time.

S3.say: I'd say we've got a few years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. I'd want the union and the farmers' groups in the same room.
S3.think: I think I'd still lose the work, just later. Five years is enough to see it coming but too short for someone slow with new things, like me, to change.
S3.do: Saves four to five hundred a month and aims to clear the mortgage early. Attends every union meeting on the issue and campaigns for a scheme before AGI lands, but carries on milking rather than retraining.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier than in the fast picture, like watching a drought on the forecast.
S3.quote: A house with no loan on it is the one thing a robot can't take.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't change Beth's view of herself as someone who won't retrain; it changes how she uses money. Paying off the house becomes her main plan. She is honest that she'd tell her daughter to follow her dream while privately worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly: a share for workers, retraining that's real, not a leaflet. I'd probably still say it at the Plough on a Thursday rather than online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels far off. I'd be 53. The mortgage would be done by then anyway, the kids would be grown or nearly. It'd still be sad, but it wouldn't be a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd mostly wait and see for the first few years and keep milking. I'd keep the union pushing and vote for whoever has a real plan for workers. And I'd keep the savings ticking over the way we do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a far-off way. It's a cloud on the hill, not over the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is there anything you'd start now that you wouldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm honest. Maybe I'd get Lily and Tom to think about what they'll do, but that's their life. For me it'd mostly mean keeping my head down and letting the union do the long fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't retrain. With a decade, is that still true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and I know how that sounds. Kev at work says I'm stubborn as a heifer at the crush gate and he's right. If something came along that was proven and local, maybe, but I wouldn't go looking.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it properly, with a share for workers and retraining that's real. I'd say it at the pub rather than online.
S4.think: Ten years feels far off to me: the mortgage would be done and the kids nearly grown. It'd still be sad, but it wouldn't be a cliff.
S4.do: Waits and sees for the first few years while carrying on milking. Keeps the union pushing, votes for a party with a real plan for workers, and keeps saving at the current rate.
S4.feel: A distant worry, more sadness than fear.
S4.quote: It's a cloud on the hill, not over the yard.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline makes Beth relax rather than plan. She admits the contradiction between wanting real retraining for workers and not wanting it herself. Her age and paid-down mortgage are what make ten years feel safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because it gets Rob and me at the same time and there's no time to get the house paid off. What would help is the government saying now, out loud, that if robots take the work, the people they replace get a share, paid like a wage. And a union that's at the table when the board buys the machines, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone asks about jobs, but a robot doesn't notice a heifer standing off on her own in the corner of the field. I'm not saying I'm better than a machine at everything, I'm saying there's things you only see because you care, and I don't know who does the caring after.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't notice a heifer standing off on her own in the corner of the field.
portrait: Beth Torres is a 43-year-old herd and field hand on Millbrook, a co-op dairy and barley farm, where she's worked for nineteen years and is a proud union member. She has good pay, solid savings and a mostly paid mortgage, but she avoids new technology and leaves app records to the office. She stays calm if AI stalls and uneasy with steady change, turning first to the union rather than to retraining. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because it would hit her and her bus-driver partner at once, and longer timelines mostly change how fast she pays down the house. She blames owners and an absent government, not the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her and her partner at the same time with no time to pay off the house.
whatWouldHelp: The government promising now that people replaced by robots get a share paid like a wage, and the union being at the table when machines are bought.
